1.pericope_label: Three years of peace, Jehoshaphat’s visit, and the resolve to recover Ramoth-gilead

schools.summary: Ellicott dates the three years from the rash peace with Benhadad and reads the silence about Ramoth-gilead as evidence that Syria has recovered its independence, the revived power sufficing to face Israel and Judah together, which justifies the prophetic rebuke that followed the treaty; he hears deference as much as friendship in Judah’s answer to the stronger kingdom, finds that its prosperity had come to depend in part on the change of policy from enmity to alliance, traces Ramoth-gilead from a place of refuge in Gad to a frontier fortress taken and retaken, and holds that the chapter as a whole shows Ahab had returned to the worship of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch reject Thenius’s dating of the visit to late in the third year, since it came before the war was renewed, and place Ramoth at the site of the modern Szalt.

Henry takes the peace for a reward: Ahab continued under guilt and wrath and under the dominion of the lusts to which he had sold himself, yet for his professions of repentance was given three years’ quiet and an honourable visit. He finds the alliance strange from both ends, that so great a man should respect a kingdom revolted from the house of David and so good a man show kindness to a king revolted from the worship of God, and lays it to a temper too easy, which betrayed him into snares; from Benhadad’s broken word he draws that the promises of an enemy are as deceitful as his kisses and that no confidence is to be placed in leagues extorted by distress; and he observes that Ahab had a good cause and did not prosper, since equity is not to be judged of by prosperity.

Gill dates the peace from Benhadad’s covenant, holds the years not three full ones but parts of them, and reports that Elijah’s threat — that Ahab’s life should go for Benhadad’s — had been respited for just this interval, Ben Gersom and others ascribing the reprieve to the king’s humiliation; he marks the piety of the king of Judah, who would not enter a war without knowing God’s pleasure.

Clarke dates the peace from the covenant of the previous chapter and supposes the treaty stipulated the city’s return; he grounds the good understanding between the two courts in the marriage alliance of Jehoshaphat’s son to Ahab’s daughter, and notes that the coalition displeased God and drew Jehu the seer’s severe reproof.

debates.question: Why did Jehoshaphat ally himself with the house of Ahab?

positions.view: Through the marriage alliance, a coalition that displeased God and was severely reproved
Through deference to the stronger kingdom, on which Judah’s prosperity had come partly to depend
Through a temper too easy, which betrayed a godly man into snares
In joining Israel against Syria he atoned for his father’s fault in joining Syria against Israel
held_by: some, as reported by Matthew Henry

outliers.claim: Alone in holding that the chapter as a whole shows Ahab had by this time returned to the worship of the Lord.
Alone in reporting, and dismissing as groundless, the rabbinic conceit that Jehoshaphat was sent for to chastise Ahab with so many stripes a day.

6.pericope_label: The four hundred prophets, Zedekiah’s iron horns, and Micaiah fetched under pressure

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from the prophets’ own words that they were neither prophets of Baal nor of the Asherah, yet that Jehoshaphat’s discontent shows them no true prophets of Jehovah either, and supposes them devoted, like the old prophet of Bethel, to the idolatry of Jeroboam; he shows what the English hides, that the four hundred had used a title which might name the supreme God of any religion, so that the request is for a prophet of Jehovah; he collects the horn as an emblem of victorious strength from Balaam to the visions of Daniel and Zechariah, reads the two thrones as an attempt to overawe the prophet with pomp and a rival inspiration, and finds in the officer’s advice the confusion common to superstition, which believes a prophet inspired and yet fancies the inspiration can be bribed. Keil and Delitzsch rule out Baal’s prophets, since by them Ahab could not have enquired the word of Jehovah, rule out equally that these were disciples of the true prophets, set the thrones on a threshing-floor before the gate, and make the horns iron spikes held on the head, embodying the blessing of Joseph so as to transfer to Ahab a promise that belonged to Ephraim.

Henry fastens on Ahab’s admission, that he granted the man a true prophet who knew God’s mind and hated him all the same, his reason being that the prophet never prophesied good concerning him — and whose fault was that? Those are wretchedly hardened who hate God’s ministers for dealing plainly. He takes the king to have known where to find him because he had imprisoned him three years before, and notes that the prison had not excluded him from divine visits: he was bound, but the word of the Lord was not. He sees a crowd of flatterers about the thrones and remarks that those who love to be flattered shall not want flatterers; thinks the officer unworthy the name of an Israelite for prescribing to a prophet; and draws from the unanimity of the four hundred that unity is not always the mark of a true church or a true ministry.

Gill follows the Targum and the Arabic in calling the four hundred false prophets, Ahab’s and not the Lord’s, and guesses they were the prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel’s table and were spared when Baal’s were destroyed, since the number agrees; he reads the iron horns as a prophetic sign and has the prophet swear by the living God.
Clarke makes the four hundred Jezebel’s prophets of Asherah, absent from the contest on Carmel, and reads the iron horns as the kind of prophecy that instructs by significant gesture.

debates.question: Who were the four hundred prophets Ahab gathered?

positions.view: False prophets of the groves, who ate at Jezebel’s table and were spared when Baal’s were destroyed
Jezebel’s prophets of Asherah, who had stayed away from the contest on Carmel
Neither Baal’s nor the Asherah’s, but men devoted to the idolatry of Jeroboam
Not Baal’s prophets, since the word of Jehovah could not be enquired by them, nor disciples of the true prophets

outliers.claim: Alone in showing that the four hundred shrank from the distinctive Name and used a title that might have meant the supreme God of any religion, which is what prompts the request for a prophet of Jehovah.
Alone in drawing from the unanimity of the four hundred that unity is not always the mark of a true church or a true ministry.

15.pericope_label: The ironic oracle, the adjuration, and the vision of Israel scattered as sheep

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the verbal agreement with the four hundred for a demonstration of how the prophet would speak if he were guided, as they were, by personal considerations, and hold that Ahab caught the irony from the tone; they also note that the king, having asked for a true word of the Lord, at once tried to put the unfavourable answer down to private enmity. Ellicott makes him a true disciple of Elijah in the defiance of the tone, mocking the false prophets so bitterly as to show his scorn of them and of the king together, yet observes that the message comes in metaphor and symbolic vision rather than Elijah’s stern directness.

Clarke calls it strong irony, spoken so as to show the king at once that he did not believe a word of it, and alone asks how the sentence could be repeated at all: the object is absent from the Hebrew, so the promise that the Lord will deliver it into the king’s hand can be read two ways with equal right, and the prophet repeats the formula precisely in order to expose its fallacy. He sets it beside the deliberately double oracles of the heathen, which saved the priest’s credit whatever the outcome, and adds that where such oracles were not ambiguous they were couched so darkly that the oracle was needed to explain the oracle. On the vision he takes the sheep without a shepherd for the defeat of Israel and the death of the king.

Henry draws the moral that those deserve to be bantered who love to be flattered, and that it is just with God to give up to their own counsels those who give themselves up to their own lusts. On the vision he has Israel deprived of the king who was their shepherd, and notices what it does not foresee, any great slaughter in the army, but only a retreat without its object, the king falling in war while the rest go home in peace. When the king turns to his guest, Henry finds the turn characteristic, since those who bear malice are generally willing to believe that others bear malice to them; and he asks what evil had in fact been prophesied, since the king was told the expedition would be fatal while still free to choose, the greatest kindness we can do to one going a dangerous way being to tell him of his danger.

Gill observes that the king had not in fact adjured him before but asks how often he must, and so adjures him once for all; and he has the king perceive plainly from the vision that he should fall in battle.

debates.question: What does the vision of the scattered sheep foretell?

positions.view: The defeat of Israel and the death of the king, the political shepherd who shall fall in battle
Not great slaughter but a dishonourable retreat, the king falling while the rest go home in peace

outliers.claim: Alone in finding the oracle ambiguous because its object is absent from the Hebrew, and in setting it beside the double-edged answers given to Croesus and to Pyrrhus.
Alone in noting that this prophet’s message comes in metaphor and symbolic vision rather than in Elijah’s stern directness.

19.pericope_label: The heavenly court and the lying spirit; Zedekiah’s blow and Micaiah’s committal

schools.summary: Ellicott begins from the article, which should give the spirit, calls the explanation that it merely anticipates the description weak, and the reading that it means the spirit of prophecy, an emanation from the Godhead, conceivable but unprecedented; he prefers, without importing the Satan of Job and Zechariah, the conception common to every religion that reckons with evil, of a spiritual power of evil overruled to work out the judgments of God. He finds in the blow on the cheek not contempt only but professed indignation at blasphemy, the gesture recorded afterwards against Christ and against Paul. Keil and Delitzsch treat the vision as the disclosure of the hidden ground of the false prophecy, and render the closing appeal not to the people present but to the nations, who were to judge it by the event.

Clarke calls the vision a mere parable, telling in figurative language what was in the womb of providence — the events shortly to come, the agents employed, and God’s permission for them to act — and adds a reason of manner: rather than tell so angry a king that his prophets were liars in whom the father of lies dwelt, the prophet said the same truths less offensively. He holds that Scripture repeatedly represents God as doing what in providence he only permits, and presses the consequence that never was a man more circumstantially warned, having counsels from the God of truth and from the spirit of falsity before him, so that his blood was upon his own head. On the blow he matches insolence to brutality in the taunt, and supposes a divine judgement overtook the striker in the inner chamber.

Gill insists the whole is represented as in a vision, brought down to the capacities of men and not as really transacted, and that the Lord did not enter into consultation with angels; he will not have the spirit from the heavenly host on either hand, since those are pure and impeccable and cannot lie, and makes it the old deceiver come forth from his own place and company; he has God suffer the lying spirit to suggest the lie and send strong delusions to believe it, and offers three readings of the inner chamber.

Henry agrees that the scene is set out after the manner of men, and that God is neither put upon new counsels nor the author of sin; he puts the permission to another use, that God thereby serves his own purposes, giving up to strong delusions those who do not receive the truth in love of it. He notes that to strike within the verge of a court is in our own law a high misdemeanour, yet this went unreprimanded, the king being pleased and Jehoshaphat wanting courage to appear for the injured man; and he has the striker shelter as Benhadad had done, lest the blind prophet fall into the ditch with the prince he had misled, ruling that those who will not have their mistakes rectified by the word of God are undeceived too late by its judgments.

debates.question: Is the vision of the throne and the host a transaction or a parable?

positions.view: A representation brought down to the capacities of men, not a thing really transacted
A further revelation disclosing the hidden ground of the false prophecy

debates.question: What is the spirit that undertakes to persuade Ahab?

positions.view: The old deceiver, come forth from his own place and company, since the heavenly host cannot lie
A spiritual power of evil overruled to work out the judgments of God, without importing the Satan of Job and Zechariah
The spirit of prophecy, an emanation from the Godhead
held_by: others, as reported and judged unprecedented by Charles Ellicott

outliers.claim: Alone in pressing that the king had counsels from the God of truth and from the spirit of falsity side by side, so that his blood was upon his own head.

29.pericope_label: The march to Ramoth-gilead, Ahab’s disguise, and the cry that saved the wrong king

schools.summary: Gill finds four things to incline the king of Judah to go: four hundred prophets agreed and used the Lord’s name and he could not confute them; the evil was prophesied of Ahab only; he had given his word; and the cause was just, being the recovery of territory. He has Ahab change his royal robes for a common soldier’s, perhaps on word brought by spies, and records Abarbinel’s view that he meant rather to put on a coat of mail and go armed; and he notes that the thirty-two captains were the number of Syria’s kings in the first war and of its captains in the second.

Keil and Delitzsch put the continued adhesion down to false shame, which kept Jehoshaphat from retracting an unconditional promise merely on an utterance Ahab had ascribed to private dislike; they hold that even Ahab could not shake off a certain fear that the prophecy would be fulfilled and find the anxiety in the grammar, a broken but strong form of the verb; and they decline Thenius’s proposal to amend the captains’ verb to the one used in Chronicles. Ellicott reads the whole subservient part Jehoshaphat plays as the mark of a virtual dependence of Judah on the stronger kingdom, of which the marriage alliance was at once the sign and the cause; calls the disguise almost ludicrously characteristic of a temper of half-belief and half-unbelief; observes that the recovered power of Syria is directed with singular virulence against the king who had unwisely spared it; and takes the cry as a rally, adding from Chronicles that God moved the captains to depart.

Henry calls the continued adhesion matter of astonishment and lays it to an easy temper carried away by the delusion of friends, adding that in his own country he had never been imposed on by such cheats. He sees two designs in the disguise, to make a liar of a good prophet and a fool of a good king, and asks how a man false to his God should be true to his friend; he holds Ahab justly repaid for sparing Benhadad, who stung the bosom that fostered him; and he reads both halves of Jehoshaphat’s peril as providence, the danger showing God’s displeasure at the confederacy, since the man who had said I am as thou art was now taken for him, and the rescue showing that he was not deserted.

Clarke supposes Ahab had heard of the orders given against his person, and alone presses the second half of the sentence: he rejects the explanation that Jehoshaphat was to appear as king of Judah because the Syrians had no quarrel with him, prefers the Greek, which turns the clause round so that Ahab tells him to put on Ahab’s own robes, and asks whether that is not what made the Syrians take Jehoshaphat for the king of Israel.

debates.question: Why did Jehoshaphat march after so plain a warning?

positions.view: Four things inclined him: the agreement of the four hundred, the evil foretold of Ahab only, his given word, and the justice of the cause
False shame, which kept him from retracting an unconditional promise
An easy temper carried away by the delusion of friends
A virtual dependence of Judah on the stronger kingdom, of which the marriage alliance was sign and cause

debates.question: What is meant by telling Jehoshaphat to put on his robes?

positions.view: He was to appear as king of Judah, with whom the Syrians had no quarrel
held_by: Jarchi (as reported, and rejected, by Adam Clarke)

positions.view: The Greek turns the clause round: Ahab tells him to put on Ahab’s own robes, which is what caused the mistake

outliers.claim: Alone in calling the disguise almost ludicrously characteristic of a temper of half-belief, absurd in itself and yet true to a nature always halting between two opinions.

34.pericope_label: The arrow at a venture, Ahab’s death in the chariot, and the dogs at the pool of Samaria

schools.summary: Clarke reads the word rendered in his simplicity as integrity, uprightness or perfection, and thinks it most probably means to the utmost of the archer’s skill and strength, implying both aim and power with his mark full in view, the bow bent until the string drew the arrow up to its head; he canvasses where it entered, offering the joint between cuirass and helmet, so through the neck, or that between cuirass and thigh-pieces, so through the abdomen, and notes the Vulgate’s reading between the lungs and the stomach. He says the king did not wish his misfortune known lest his troops be discouraged, observes that the Greek version renders the disputed clause of the harlots bathing and that the Hebrew will bear it, and places the ivory house in Samaria, recalling that Amos denounced such luxury.

Gill has the archer neither aiming at the king nor knowing whereabout he was, and names him from the Targum and Jarchi as Naaman, the Syrian general; he keeps to the plain sense of the washing, having the charioteer drive the vehicle into the pool to cleanse it of his master’s blood, and suspects the ivory house was inlaid rather than built of ivory.

Ellicott also finds the archer named in Josephus, grants that Ahab’s imperfect repentance at least secured him a warrior’s death before the evil came upon his house, and remarks that the union of desperate physical courage with moral feebleness is common in history and, as Shakespeare delighted to show, true to nature; he thinks there is little doubt that the harlots bathed in the bloodstained pool, the dog and the harlot being the animal and the human types of uncleanness, and raises the difficulty that a later notice places the requital in Naboth’s field at Jezreel. He notices too that this is the first mention of ivory for inlaying walls since Solomon’s day, an art characteristic of Zidon. Keil and Delitzsch have the king keep upright on the chariot before the Syrians so as not to dishearten his soldiers, render the conflict as a rising stream, call the disputed clause a circumstantial one whose verb means to bathe, hold that the only tenable explanation, and say it disposes of the emendations Thenius favours.

Henry takes the wound for the one place about the king where the arrow could find entrance, and concludes that no armour is proof against the darts of divine vengeance; he has him held up to see whether his army prevailed, his spirits sinking as the battle goes against them, the death lingering enough that he had time to feel himself die and to see the iron horns pushing not the Syrians but himself into destruction; he notes that the dogs made no difference between royal blood and other, and supposes the ivory house meant to vie with Solomon’s palace.

debates.question: Was the fatal shot aimless or drawn at full stretch?

positions.view: At a venture, the archer neither aiming at the king nor knowing whereabout he was
To the utmost of his skill and strength, with his mark full in view

debates.question: Does the clause mean that they washed his armour, or that the harlots bathed in the pool?

positions.view: The harlots bathed there; the verb means to bathe and the clause is circumstantial
The plain sense of a washing, the chariot being driven into the pool to cleanse it

outliers.claim: Alone in raising the difficulty that a later notice places the requital in Naboth’s field at Jezreel, and in judging the reconcilement difficult if not impossible while holding that the clearer reference here must outweigh it.

41.pericope_label: Jehoshaphat’s reign: the high places, the long peace, Edom’s deputy, and the wrecked Ophir fleet

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the brevity of the notice: the narrative keeps to the prophetic work in Israel, and the compiler gives only a few annalistic notices of the southern kingdom, where Chronicles gives a full account of the reign and its great religious revival, with which the notices of his might and his wars agree entirely. He finds the key to the high places in the accompanying words about the groves, holds the verse about the peace chronologically out of place, identifies the subject ally later called a king of Edom with the deputy of this passage, and supplies from Chronicles the combined fleet and the prophet who denounced the alliance. Keil and Delitzsch note that he kept peace with every Israelite king of his lifetime, where the kingdoms had been hostile before, and call that laudable though he went beyond what was allowable in the marriage alliance; they hold the notice of a deputy inserted only to explain how ships could be built in Edomite territory, and add that he could not expect a better result from a second attempt once the prediction was fulfilled.

Clarke distinguishes two kinds of high place, those used for idolatry, which were removed, and those consecrated to God before the temple was built, which were left; failing that, he suspects the parallel text is corrupt, a single letter having turned he did not take away into moreover he took away. He infers from the notice about Edom that the compiler wrote after the revolt of the next reign, takes the clearing of the consecrated persons to be aimed at a system rather than at men, and alone refuses the refusal of the second voyage, reading the two words that differ by one letter and sound alike as he consented to him while conceding that no manuscript supports it.

Henry calls the reign none of the longest but one of the best, and adds its twenty-five years to his father’s forty-one to show how long Judah flourished; he finds a compensation in its brevity, since the king was spared the blemishes that marked his father’s last years, and it is better to die in the midst of a reputation than to outlive it. He does not reconcile the texts about the high places but moralises the fact, that every man’s character has its but, and that these stood even in the tribes nearest Jerusalem, old corruptions being hard to root out when they have had the patronage of good men; and he reads the wrecked fleet as a rebuke for the league, the rod of God expounded by his word having broken the king off from it.

Gill does the arithmetic of the reign, eighteen years alongside Ahab and seven after him, agrees that the notice of a deputy explains how ships could be built in Edomite territory, and reads the clearing of the consecrated persons as finishing what the previous reign had left undone.

debates.question: How are the two statements about the high places to be reconciled?

positions.view: Two kinds are in view — the idolatrous removed, those consecrated to God before the temple left — or else the parallel text is corrupt, a single letter having reversed its sense
What was removed were the high places of the Asherah worship; merely unauthorised sanctuaries remained in part
The texts are not reconciled but the fact moralised: every character has its blemish

debates.question: Did Jehoshaphat refuse the second voyage?

positions.view: He refused, the wreck and the prophet’s word having broken him off from the alliance
The words should be read he consented to him, though no manuscript supports it

outliers.claim: Alone in proposing a one-letter emendation that reverses the refusal, and in endorsing Houbigant’s rearrangement moving the note that the ships never sailed to the end of the following verse.

themes: a good reign with a blemish

51.pericope_label: Ahaziah succeeds Ahab and revives the worship of Baal

schools.summary: Gill shows that the accession date does not add up: if the king of Judah began in Ahab’s fourth year and Ahab reigned twenty-two, then Ahab’s son should begin in the eighteenth of Judah rather than the seventeenth. He offers two ways out, that the son was made king during his father’s lifetime before the expedition to Ramoth-gilead, or that the twenty-two years were not complete; and he reduces the evil of the reign to the one word idolatry, the son serving Baal as his father had done and his mother still did.

Ellicott finds in the short reign the revival of an influence that had been in abeyance during Ahab’s last days, the Baal worship resuming its place beside the older idolatry of the calves and presently beside the worship of the Canaanitish Baalzebub as well. Keil and Delitzsch divide the inheritance between the parents who had brought Baal into the kingdom and the king who had set up the calves, note that the adoration of Baal is then stated again expressly, and object that closing both the chapter and the book with this general description is very unsuitable, since the rest of the reign and the king’s death are related at the opening of the next book.

Henry marks the brevity itself, not two years, and that some sinners God makes quick work with; he lays the blame on both parents, since the son took no warning but followed his father’s example and his more wicked mother’s counsel, she being still alive. Miserable, he says, are the children who not only derive a sinful nature from their parents but are taught by them to increase it, and most unhappy the parents who help to damn their children’s souls; hardened sinners press on unmoved along the road by which others before them were driven into misery.

outliers.claim: Alone in objecting to where the account stops, holding that a fresh chapter, and the second book with it, should have begun at the verse that states the king’s evil.
Alone in noticing that the regnal arithmetic yields the eighteenth year of Judah rather than the seventeenth, and in offering two ways to account for it.
